hints: Compare the steepness of the two lines in Fig. 2.1 between $5^{\circ}C$ and $20^{\circ}C$ - where does temperature make a big difference and where does it make almost no difference?
Remember that photosynthesis has a light-dependent stage and an enzyme-controlled Calvin cycle - which stage needs light directly and which stage needs enzymes?
Think about what higher temperature does to molecules - how does molecular movement affect how often enzymes meet their substrates?
Link the two observations together using the idea of a limiting factor - when one thing is in short supply, changing something else has little effect.
walkthrough:
Describe What You See in Fig. 2.1**
Look closely at the two lines. The high light intensity line rises steeply as temperature goes from $5^{\circ}C$ to $20^{\circ}C$. The low light intensity line stays almost flat over the same range. So temperature has a large effect when light is plentiful, but almost no effect when light is low.

Why Temperature Speeds Up Photosynthesis**
Much of photosynthesis, especially the Calvin cycle, depends on enzymes such as Rubisco. Warming gives all molecules more kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate molecules move faster and collide more often. That means more enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time, so the Calvin cycle runs faster and fixes more carbon dioxide.

Why Light Intensity Changes the Effect - Limiting Factors**
A limiting factor is the one factor in shortest supply that holds back the rate. At high light intensity there is plenty of ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent stage, so the enzyme-controlled Calvin cycle holds back the rate and temperature is limiting. At low light intensity there is too little light to make ATP and reduced NADP, so light is limiting and warming the enzymes cannot increase the rate.

Final answer: At high light intensity, rate increases steeply with temperature from $5$ to $20^{\circ}C$; at low light intensity there is little increase. Increased temperature gives increased kinetic energy, increasing collisions / enzyme-substrate complex formation and enzyme activity in the Calvin cycle. At high light, temperature is limiting; at low light, light intensity is limiting.

hints: Think about what is being measured on the y-axis for each curve in Fig. 2.2 - one is a physical uptake of light, the other is a biological output.
Focus on the x-axis shared by both - wavelength in $nm$ - and state clearly what is plotted against wavelength in each case.
walkthrough:
Absorption Spectrum - What Pigments Take In**
Imagine shining each colour of light, from violet at $400 nm$ to red at $700 nm$, onto extracted pigments and measuring how much is absorbed. That plot of absorbance against wavelength is the absorption spectrum. It tells you which colours chlorophyll and other pigments capture best.

Action Spectrum - What the Plant Does With It**
Now imagine shining each colour onto a whole leaf or plant and measuring how fast it photosynthesises, for example by oxygen release. That plot of rate of photosynthesis against wavelength is the action spectrum. It tells you which colours actually drive photosynthesis fastest.
Final answer: Absorption spectrum: absorbance / absorption of different wavelengths of light by chloroplast pigments. Action spectrum: rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths of light.

hints: Look at the peaks and troughs in Fig. 2.2 - both curves are high in blue and red light around $430 nm$ and $680 nm$ and low in green around $550 nm$.
Think causally - if a pigment cannot absorb a wavelength, can that light energy enter photosynthesis?
walkthrough:
Absorbed Energy Drives the Work**
Only light that is absorbed can be used. Photons captured by pigments excite electrons in photosystems, leading to ATP and reduced NADP formation for the Calvin cycle. Light that is reflected or transmitted, like much green light, cannot do this work.

Matching Peaks Mean Matching Function**
That is why the two curves rise and fall together. Where absorbance is high, in blue and red regions, more energy enters the system so the rate of photosynthesis is high. Where absorbance is low, in green-yellow around $500-600 nm$, little energy enters so the rate is low.
Final answer: Light energy absorbed by pigments is used to drive photosynthesis; wavelengths absorbed most strongly give the highest rate of photosynthesis, so peaks and troughs match.

hints: Remember that only the primary pigment chlorophyll a at the reaction centre can pass an excited electron to the electron transport chain - so what must other pigments do with the energy they catch?
Think about why having several different pigments is useful - do they all absorb exactly the same colours as chlorophyll a?
walkthrough:
Catching More Light and Funnelling It In**
Think of chlorophyll a in the reaction centre as the only door into electron transport. Accessory pigments like carotene and chlorophyll b form a light-harvesting antenna complex around it. When they absorb a photon, they become excited and pass that excitation energy by resonance directly to chlorophyll a at the reaction centre.

Broadening the Spectrum**
This teamwork is powerful because carotene absorbs different wavelengths, especially in the blue-green region, that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly. By harvesting extra colours and feeding the energy inward, accessory pigments let the plant use more of the visible spectrum for photosynthesis.

Final answer: Accessory pigment absorbs light of wavelengths not absorbed by chlorophyll a / reaction centre and passes energy to chlorophyll a / primary pigment / reaction centre as part of light-harvesting antenna complex / photosystem.
